title: The Mu'allaqa of Amr ibn Kulthum
intro: Amr ibn Kulthum, chief of the tribe of Taghlib, composed it. Ibn al-Anbari relates that Taghlib and its brother tribe Bakr ibn Wa'il took a quarrel before Amr ibn Hind, king of al-Hira, that al-Harith ibn Hilliza recited his own poem for Bakr, and that Amr then recited this one, and “when he had finished, people thought nothing could equal it”; al-Aghani connects it instead with his killing of the king, who had tried to make the poet's mother wait on his own. It opens with a call for the morning wine, bids farewell to a departing beloved and describes her, then turns on the king and on Bakr with a long boast of Taghlib's battles, ancestors, horses and women, ending with tyrants falling prostrate before a Taghlib child. Al-Aghani says the tribe revered it so much, young and old reciting it, that a poet of Bakr mocked them for it, and al-Zirikli reports that it is said to have run to about a thousand lines, of which only what the transmitters remembered survives. The recensions differ widely in the number and order of the lines, and this recitation gathers lines from several of them.

translation: Up, girl, with your wide bowl, and pour us our morning wine;
do not hold back the wines of al-Andarin.
1.sharh: He wakes the woman who serves the wine and asks for the morning draught, poured from the large bowl. She is not to keep the wines of al-Andarin for others and give them something lesser: they want the best.

translation: Mixed with water, as if saffron-flower were in it
when the water blends with it, and we grow generous.
2.sharh: He wants the wine thinned with water and red as saffron-flower, and once they drink it they turn open-handed. The commentators also read sakhina as “hot”: the wine is mixed with warm water.

translation: It turns a man with a need away from his desire
once he tastes it, till he softens.
3.sharh: The wine turns a man away from the business that weighs on him: one taste and he unbends, forgets his cares and gives himself to his companions. Al-Tibrizi glosses the softening as leaving his desire behind and growing calm.

translation: You see the tight-fisted miser, when it is passed to him,
squandering his wealth on it.
4.sharh: Even a mean and narrow man, once the cup comes round to him, spends his money freely on wine. Ibn al-Anbari adds that drink also mends his temper: the sour, grasping man turns open-handed and pleasant.

translation: It is as if flames were in their ears
when they knock its rim against their foreheads.
5.sharh: When they drain the cup so far that its rim knocks their foreheads, the wine flushes their ears red as burning brands. The line is found in the Jamhara, not in the classical commentaries.

translation: You turned the cup away from us, Umm Amr,
and the cup's course should have run to the right.
6.sharh: He complains to the woman pouring, Umm Amr, that she has steered the cup away from him, though custom passes it round to the right and his turn has come. Al-Tibrizi reads “you held back the cup”.

translation: Umm Amr, the one of the three you pass over
for the morning wine is not the worst of them.
7.sharh: Of the three drinkers she serves, the one she leaves without his morning cup, the poet himself, is not the least deserving. It is mock reproach: he claims his rightful turn. Al-Tibrizi notes that some ascribe this line and the one before to another Amr, the nephew of Jadhima al-Abrash.

translation: Many a cup I have drunk in Baalbek,
and another in Damascus and Qasirin.
8.sharh: After reproaching the woman who passed him over, he recalls the cups he has drunk across Syria, in Baalbek, Damascus and Qasirin: he is no stranger to good wine, and deserves his turn at hers.

translation: When its strength makes for a sober, sensible
young man, you would think him mad.
9.sharh: The wine is strong enough to make the most level-headed young man behave like a madman, robbing him of his composure, as a note in the Jamhara explains. The line is one the Jamhara adds to the commentators' text.

translation: It kept going round the drinkers' circle until
they vied for it, and said, “We have had our fill.”
10.sharh: The wine went round and round while the drinkers outbid one another for it, until at last they declared themselves satisfied. One printed edition of the Jamhara has the opposite in its text, “we have not had our fill”.

translation: Death will overtake us,
fated for us, and we fated for it.
11.sharh: Death will come for them all: it is decreed for them and they for it. The line ties back to the opening, as al-Tibrizi explains: pour the wine now, before death arrives.

translation: Stop before we part, woman in the litter,
and we will tell you the truth, and you tell us.
12.sharh: He calls on the departing woman in her camel litter to halt for a moment, so that each may tell the other what has happened since they parted. The love section of the poem begins here.

translation: Stop, so we can ask: have you broken it off
because the parting came so soon, or betrayed one you could trust?
13.sharh: He asks whether the haste of the parting has made her cut him off, or whether she has betrayed a lover who never betrayed her. Ibn al-Anbari's text reads “have you formed a new bond”.

translation: Of a day of battle, of striking and thrusting,
that brought joy to the eyes of your kinsmen.
14.sharh: What he wants to tell her is the news of a hard-fought day of sword and spear, a victory that gave her kinsmen everything they wished for. To “cool the eyes” is to give someone joy.

translation: Tomorrow, and today, are in pledge,
and the day after, to what you do not know.
15.sharh: Every day, present and to come, is bound to events no one can foresee. The Jamhara's commentary reads it as a lover's line: he has given his heart to this woman and cannot tell what fate holds for her.

translation: She shows you, when you come to her alone
and she is safe from the eyes of those who hate her,
16.sharh: When he finds her alone, out of sight of the ill-wishers, she lets him see the beauties the next lines list. The sentence runs on: what she shows him is the object of the following lines.

translation: Arms like those of a long-necked she-camel, white, young,
pure of colour, that has never carried a foal,
17.sharh: She shows him arms as full and white as those of a young, long-necked she-camel. Al-Zawzani explains that a camel which has never carried young is plump, so the detail stresses how full her arms are.

translation: And a breast like an ivory casket, soft,
untouched by the hands of those who would touch.
18.sharh: He praises her breast as white and round as a small ivory box, and soft, and stresses her chastity: no hand has ever touched it. Beauty joined to virtue is what he will praise again in the women of his tribe near the end.

translation: And a throat like the light of the full moon when it rises
at its fullest on people under cloud.
19.sharh: Her throat and breast shine like the full moon breaking on travellers lost under a clouded sky, so that they can see their way. The Jamhara, the source of this line, makes the travellers simply night-walkers.

translation: And the back of a supple body, tall and towering,
its hips weighing down what lies near them.
20.sharh: Her figure is tall and pliant, and her hips so full that they seem to drag on the rest of her as she rises: al-Zawzani sums it up as a tall stature and heavy hips.

translation: And haunches the door is too narrow for,
and a waist that has driven me mad.
21.sharh: Her haunches are too wide for a doorway, her waist slender enough to drive him mad. Al-Zawzani says the door is too narrow for her because of how full and fleshy her hips are.

translation: And two columns of ivory or marble
whose jingling ornaments ring out.
22.sharh: Her legs are like pillars of ivory or marble, white and full, and her anklets chime as she moves. The Jamhara's version speaks of the sides of her neck instead.

translation: No she-camel grieved as I grieve, for a calf
she lost, and then kept up her moaning,
23.sharh: His grief at the parting outdoes that of a camel that has lost her newborn calf and keeps moaning for it. The comparison is the first of two; the next line adds a still sharper sorrow.

translation: nor a grey-haired woman whose misery left her
of nine sons only the buried.
24.sharh: Nor did an old mother who has buried all nine of her sons grieve as he does. The two comparisons, the camel and the bereaved mother, mark the height of his sorrow at the parting.

translation: I remembered my youthful love and longed, when
I saw her laden camels driven off at evening,
25.sharh: The sight of her baggage camels being driven off in the late afternoon brought back his youthful passion and his longing. The Jamhara has “I went back to my youth”, to the follies he had given up.

translation: and al-Yamama came into view and towered up
like swords in the hands of men who have drawn them.
26.sharh: The villages of al-Yamama rose into view, glinting in the shimmering haze like swords drawn from their scabbards, as al-Zawzani and Ibn al-Anbari explain. The sight marks how far her caravan has gone.

translation: Abu Hind, do not rush to judge us:
give us time and we will tell you the truth.
27.sharh: Here the poem turns to the king, Amr ibn Hind, called by his kunya Abu Hind: let him not be hasty, but hear the truth about the tribe of Taghlib. The boast that fills the rest of the poem begins.

translation: that we lead our banners in white to the water
and bring them back red, drenched.
28.sharh: The truth he promised: Taghlib's banners go into battle white and come back red, soaked with the enemy's blood. The verbs are those for leading animals down to water and back.

translation: and of famous, long days of ours
when we defied the king rather than submit.
29.sharh: He reminds the king of Taghlib's celebrated battle days, “days” meaning battles, when they refused to obey a king. Abu Ubayda, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari, says they were bright for Taghlib and long for its enemies.

translation: And many a lord of his people, whom they crowned
with a king's crown, who protected those driven to refuge,
30.sharh: Taghlib has brought down crowned kings who were themselves the protectors of others. The sentence runs on into the next line, where the king lies dead and the horses stand over him.

translation: We left the horses standing round him,
their reins hung on their necks, resting on three legs.
31.sharh: Having killed the crowned lord, they left the horses standing over him with their reins looped on their necks. Al-Tibrizi reads it either as Taghlib's riders dismounting to strip him, or as his own people's horses standing by, unable to help.

translation: We pitched our tents at Dhu Tuluh,
out to al-Shamat, driving off those who threatened.
32.sharh: Taghlib camped where it pleased, from Dhu Tuluh as far as al-Shamat, and drove away everyone who had threatened it. In the recited version the tents themselves drive off the threateners.

translation: The dogs of the camp have snarled at us,
and we have stripped the thorns from the tragacanth of our neighbours.
33.sharh: Armed for war, they looked so strange that their own camp dogs growled at them, and they have broken the strength of every neighbouring enemy. Trimming the thorny bush is a figure for blunting a foe.

translation: Whenever we move our millstone to a people,
they are its flour when we meet.
34.sharh: War is Taghlib's millstone: whatever people it is moved against are ground into flour. Having called war a mill, al-Zawzani notes, he calls its dead the flour, and the image runs on into the next line.

translation: Its leather mat will be the east of Najd,
and its handful of grain all of Quda'a.
35.sharh: Completing the image: the battlefield in eastern Najd is the mat spread under the millstone, and the whole tribe of Quda'a the handful of grain fed into it. Ibn al-Anbari also gives the reading “east of Salma”.

translation: You came to us as guests come,
so we hurried the meal, lest you revile us.
36.sharh: Sarcastic hospitality: the enemy arrived like guests, so Taghlib served them their supper at once, death in battle, so that no one could accuse it of being a slow host. Al-Zawzani calls it mockery.

translation: We gave you our hospitality, we hurried your meal
just before dawn: a crushing, grinding rock.
37.sharh: The “meal” was a dawn raid that fell on them like a boulder and ground them down. Al-Zawzani says the crushing stone stands for a war that destroyed them utterly; the dawn is the classic hour of attack.

translation: We are generous to our people and keep our hands off theirs,
and we carry for them whatever they lay on us.
38.sharh: Taghlib shares its wealth with its kin, never touches theirs, and shoulders their burdens: the blood-money and obligations they lay on it. Ibn al-Anbari's text has “we have always fended off their enemies”.

translation: We thrust with spears while men keep their distance,
and strike with swords when they close in.
39.sharh: Taghlib fights at every range: spears for an enemy who keeps away, swords when he comes close. Abu Ja'far, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari, compares Zuhayr's hero, who spears when the enemy shoots and strikes when they spear.

translation: with dark spears of al-Khatt, supple,
slender, or with white swords that mow down.
40.sharh: Their weapons are the supple dark spears of al-Khatt and white swords that cut men down like grass. Al-Zawzani notes that a dark shaft shows the cane ripened fully before it was cut.

translation: With them we split the heads of men in two,
and give them the necks for grass, and they mow.
41.sharh: Their swords split skulls and treat necks as fodder to be cut. The verb for mowing grass runs through this line and the last; al-Zawzani's text has “we sickle the necks”.

translation: The skulls of the champions among them seem
camel-loads tumbling on the stony ground.
42.sharh: The heads of the enemy's champions, struck off, fall like loads slipping off camels onto rocky ground: heavy, many and scattered. Al-Zawzani says he likens the heads to loads for their size.

translation: Rancour upon rancour shows
against you, and brings out the buried sickness.
43.sharh: Grudge piled on grudge will not stay hidden: it comes out and drags the long-buried hatred into the open, which, al-Zawzani says, drives men to revenge. Al-Tibrizi and the Jamhara read “spreads” for “shows”.

translation: We inherited glory, as Ma'add well knows;
we fight for it with spears until it stands clear.
44.sharh: Their nobility is inherited, as all the tribes of Ma'add know, and they defend it with their spears until no one can doubt it. Abu Ja'far, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari, reads it as fighting until the glory is cut off from others and theirs alone.

translation: And when the tent poles fall
from the baggage camels, we defend those near us.
45.sharh: When panic strikes and the tents come crashing down off the camels in the rush to flee, Taghlib stands its ground and protects its neighbours. With Ibn al-Anbari's “onto the baggage” the tents fall on the household goods.

translation: We cut off their heads without pity,
and they do not know what to guard against.
46.sharh: Taghlib's attack is merciless, so the enemy cannot tell which blow to fear: death, the capture of their women or the loss of their wealth. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Tibrizi read “we slice off their heads”.

translation: Our swords, among us and among them,
are like twisted cloths in the hands of boys at play.
47.sharh: Swords in this fight are swung as carelessly and quickly as the knotted cloths boys hit each other with. Al-Tibrizi records that because the line grants the enemy swords too, some called the poem “the fair one”.

translation: Our clothes and theirs look
as though dyed or daubed with purple.
48.sharh: The fight is so bloody that the clothes of both sides look dyed or painted with purple-red. As in the line before, the poet counts the enemy in: the blood is on everyone, a mark of how hard both sides fought.

translation: When a tribe falters at advancing,
dreading a terror likely to come,
49.sharh: When other tribes hesitate to advance, afraid of a disaster that seems about to happen, Taghlib steps forward. Al-Tibrizi explains the dread as fear lest the terror come true; the main clause follows in the next line.

translation: we set up a mass like Rahwa, sharp-edged,
to guard our honour, and we were first.
50.sharh: Where others hold back, Taghlib sets up a battle line as solid as a mountain and bristling with weapons, to protect its good name, and wins the race to the fight.

translation: with young men who count being killed a glory,
and grey-heads tried in war.
51.sharh: Taghlib's ranks combine young men who think death in battle an honour and older men seasoned by many wars: the fire of youth and the skill of age. Al-Zawzani's text has “with youths” for “with young men”.

translation: We challenge all people, every one,
fighting their sons in defence of our sons.
52.sharh: Taghlib throws down its challenge to all mankind and meets the enemy's sons with the sword to shield its own children, as al-Zawzani explains. The rare word hudayya means a challenge.

translation: On a day when we fear for them,
our horses are out in bands, troop on troop.
53.sharh: When the women and children are in danger, Taghlib's cavalry spreads out in troops in every direction to keep the enemy away from them, as al-Zawzani explains the line.

translation: And on a day when we do not fear for them,
we press our raid home, armed and ready.
54.sharh: When the families are safe, Taghlib rides out far on the attack, fully armed. Ibn al-Anbari's version arranges the pair differently: raiding on the day of danger, sitting at ease in their gatherings on the safe day.

translation: under a chief of the Banu Jusham ibn Bakr,
with whom we pound the plains and the rough ground.
55.sharh: Taghlib's raids are led by a chief of the poet's own clan, Jusham ibn Bakr, and they trample everything in their path, every enemy, feeble or mighty.

translation: Let no tribes think
that we have weakened, that we have flagged.
56.sharh: Let no one imagine that Taghlib has been broken or grown slack. Al-Zawzani reads it as a statement, “the tribes do not know us to have weakened”, because it never happened; the reciter's vowel makes it a warning.

translation: Let no one act the fool against us,
or we will outdo the fools in folly.
57.sharh: Whoever wrongs Taghlib will be paid back worse than he gave. The commentators explain that the revenge is called “folly” only to match the word: the Quran calls the punishment of a bad deed “a bad deed like it”.

translation: What can you mean by it, Amr ibn Hind,
that we should be servants to your viceroy?
58.sharh: He demands of the king how he could ever want Taghlib to serve a lesser ruler appointed over them. Al-Zawzani explains: Taghlib has shown no weakness that could tempt the king to humble it.

translation: What can you mean by it, Amr ibn Hind,
that you heed the slanderers against us and scorn us?
59.sharh: The second question: why does the king listen to the talebearers against Taghlib and treat it with contempt? Ibn Qutayba quotes this line, with line 61, as said over the killing of Amr ibn Hind.

translation: What can you mean by it, Amr ibn Hind,
to think that we are the lowest of men?
60.sharh: A third question in the same mould: how can the king take Taghlib for the meanest of people? The line is not in the classical commentaries; the editor of the Sharh al-Mu'allaqat al-Tis' adds it in brackets.

translation: Threaten us and menace us, but gently:
when were we ever servants to your mother?
61.sharh: He tells the king to go easy with his threats: Taghlib never served his mother. The line touches on the story told of the killing, that the king wanted the poet's mother to wait on his own mother, Hind.

translation: Our spear-shaft, Amr, has refused
to bend for enemies before you.
62.sharh: Taghlib's might, pictured as a spear shaft too hard to bend, has resisted every enemy before this king, and will resist him. The image is worked out over the next two lines.

translation: When the straightening-iron bites on it, it bristles
and turns on them, hard and kicking.
63.sharh: When anyone tries to straighten this spear shaft in the clamp, it resists and turns on him, hard and recalcitrant. Al-Zawzani: the shaft no one can straighten stands for Taghlib's might, which nothing can shake.

translation: Hard, and when it is turned, it twangs,
and gashes the nape and brow of the man straightening it.
64.sharh: The shaft creaks in protest and springs back to wound whoever works on it, front and back: whoever tries to break Taghlib's pride will be hurt. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Tibrizi have “crushes” for “gashes”.

translation: Have you ever heard of Jusham ibn Bakr
falling short, in the affairs of the ancients?
65.sharh: Has the king ever heard of the poet's clan failing in anything, or breaking a pledge, in all its past? The question means it never has, and it opens the roll of ancestors that follows.

translation: We inherited the glory of Alqama ibn Sayf,
who opened the fortresses of glory to us by force.
66.sharh: The roll of ancestors begins: Alqama ibn Sayf won glory by conquest and left it open to his descendants. Al-Tibrizi reports that he is said to have settled Taghlib in al-Jazira.

translation: I inherited Muhalhil, and one better than he,
Zuhayr: the finest treasure a man could store.
67.sharh: He claims the glory of Muhalhil, his mother's father, and of Zuhayr, whom al-Zawzani takes as the better of the two. Glory inherited from forefathers is a treasure laid up for boasting.

translation: And Attab and Kulthum, both together:
through them we came into the heritage of the noblest.
68.sharh: The list goes on with Attab, the poet's great-grandfather, and Kulthum, his father: through them Taghlib holds the legacy of the noblest men. Ibn al-Anbari's text reads “the deeds of the noblest”.

translation: And Dhu al-Bura, of whom you have heard:
by him we are protected and protect those who seek refuge.
69.sharh: Dhu al-Bura, a famous chief of Taghlib, is another ancestor whose name both shields the tribe and lets it shelter others. Al-Tibrizi adds that some identify him as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr.

translation: And before him, of ours, was Kulayb, the striver:
what glory is there that we have not held?
70.sharh: The roll ends with Kulayb, Muhalhil's brother, who strove for every distinction. The question means there is no kind of glory Taghlib has not held; Ibn al-Anbari records a dispute over the case of “which”.

translation: Whenever our she-camel is tied with a rope to another,
she snaps the rope or breaks her partner's neck.
71.sharh: A camel yoked to another breaks free or breaks its partner: so Taghlib, matched against anyone in war or argument, overpowers them. Ibn al-Anbari reads the verbs as “we”: we cut the rope or break the partner.

translation: We are found the staunchest of them in guarding our charge,
and the truest to an oath once sworn.
72.sharh: Taghlib is the most reliable of the tribes: no one under its protection is harmed, and it never breaks a sworn pact, as al-Zawzani explains. Keeping one's word was the core of tribal honour.

translation: And we, on the morning the fire was lit at Khazaza,
gave help beyond the help of all who helped.
73.sharh: At the battle of Khazaza, when the beacon fire was lit, Taghlib gave more than anyone to the common cause of Nizar against the Yemenis, as al-Zawzani explains. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Tibrizi read the name Khazaz.

translation: And we held our ground at Dhu Urata
till the great milch-camels were cropping dry stubble.
74.sharh: At Dhu Urata, Taghlib kept its herds in place, even when the best camels had nothing left to eat but old dry grass, rather than retreat; Abu Ja'far, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari, reads it as holding the frontier patiently until victory.

translation: We are the judges when we are obeyed,
and resolute when we are defied.
75.sharh: Taghlib rules over those who submit to it, restraining and protecting them, and acts on its resolve against those who resist. The next lines continue the list of what “we” are.

translation: We are the ones who leave what we dislike,
and the ones who take what we please.
76.sharh: No one can force on Taghlib what it rejects, or keep from it what it wants: that, says Ibn al-Anbari, is the measure of its power and its standing among the tribes.

translation: We held the right wing when we met the foe,
and our brothers held the left.
77.sharh: In the line of battle Taghlib took the right wing and their brother tribe the left. Tha'lab takes the right as the place of honour; Ibn al-Sikkit says the battle meant is Khazaza.

translation: They charged once against those facing them,
and we charged once against those facing us.
78.sharh: Both wings attacked at once, each against the enemy opposite: the brother tribe on its side, Taghlib on its own. Ibn al-Anbari says the verb for charging comes from a stallion rearing at a rival.

translation: They came back with plunder and captives,
and we came back with kings in chains.
79.sharh: The brother tribe returned with booty and captive women; Taghlib returned with captured kings in fetters. Al-Zawzani sums it up: they took the goods, we took the kings, the nobler prize.

translation: Keep away, sons of Bakr, keep away:
have you not learned the truth about us?
80.sharh: He turns on Bakr, Taghlib's rival before the king: keep away, for you already know from experience how Taghlib fights, and should not try to rival it, as al-Zawzani explains.

translation: Have you not learned, from us and from you,
of squadrons thrusting at each other and shooting?
81.sharh: He reminds Bakr of the wars fought between the two tribes, squadron against squadron, with spear and arrow: they have felt Taghlib's strength before. Al-Tibrizi and al-Zawzani read “know” for “learn”.

translation: We lead the horses, bleeding at the flanks,
to the enemy, lean in the belly.
82.sharh: Taghlib drives its horses hard against the enemy until they are lean and bloodied. The commentators do not explain the bleeding; the likelier sense is that their flanks are raw from long, hard riding. The line is one the Jamhara adds.

translation: We wear helmets and Yemeni leather armour,
and swords that straighten and bend.
83.sharh: They go into battle in helmets and Yemeni leather armour, with swords that bend under the blows and spring straight again, so long and hard is the fighting.

translation: We wear long, gleaming coats of mail
that you see wrinkled above the belt.
84.sharh: Their mail coats are so long and ample that they fold in rumples above the belt. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Tibrizi have “above the sword-belt”, the Jamhara “below” it.

translation: When it is taken off the champions one day,
you see the warriors' skin turned black by it.
85.sharh: They wear their armour so constantly that when they do take it off, their skin is blackened by the iron; al-Zawzani explains “by it” as “from wearing it”.

translation: Their rumples are like the surface of pools
slapped by the winds as they blow.
86.sharh: The folds and rings of the mail ripple like the face of a pond ruffled by the wind, as al-Zawzani explains. Ibn al-Anbari's text has “their surfaces” instead of “their rumples”.

translation: On the morning of terror we are carried by short-haired horses,
known as ours, rescued from enemies, weaned among us.
87.sharh: Their war-horses are thoroughbreds with short coats, famous as Taghlib's: some were won back from the enemy, and all were weaned and raised in the tribe, as al-Zawzani explains.

translation: They went in armoured and came out dishevelled,
worn like the knots of reins.
88.sharh: The horses went into battle in their armour and came out tangled and worn out, like the knotted reins on their heads. The line is in al-Zawzani and the Jamhara.

translation: We inherited them from fathers true to their word,
and when we die our sons will inherit them.
89.sharh: Their horses are an old family line, handed down from honourable fathers and to be handed on to their sons. Al-Zawzani says the breed has been bred and raised in the tribe since ancient times.

translation: Behind us are fair, white women
we guard against being shared out or shamed.
90.sharh: Their women follow them into battle, and the fear of seeing them divided as spoils or dishonoured keeps the men fighting. Al-Zawzani says the Arabs brought their women to war for exactly that reason.

translation: They have made their husbands swear
that, when they meet squadrons marked out for battle,
91.sharh: The women have bound their husbands by oath that, facing enemy squadrons wearing the badges of champions, they will stand firm and not flee, as al-Zawzani explains; the oath itself follows in the next line.

translation: “You will carry off horses and swords,
and captives bound together in iron.”
92.sharh: The oath, in the women's own words: the men are to strip the enemy of horses and swords and bring home captives chained together. Ibn al-Anbari reports al-Mufaddal, through al-Farra', as saying this line is not part of the poem.

translation: You see us out in the open, while every tribe
has taken fear of us for its constant companion.
93.sharh: Taghlib camps in the open desert without fear, trusting its strength, while every other tribe lives in dread of it and seeks protection elsewhere, as al-Zawzani explains.

translation: When they walk out at evening, slow and easy,
they sway like the bodies of men who have drunk.
94.sharh: The women of the tribe walk with a slow, unhurried gait because their hips are heavy, and sway as they go like men tipsy with wine, as al-Zawzani explains.

translation: They feed our horses and say, “You are not
our husbands if you do not defend us.”
95.sharh: The women feed the war-horses themselves and goad the men: whoever fails to protect them from capture is no husband of theirs. Protection is made the condition of marriage.

translation: If we do not defend them, may we not live
for anything after them, nor stay alive.
96.sharh: The men answer the women's challenge: if they fail to protect them, may they not outlive them. Abu Ja'far, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari, calls the line spurious, though other transmitters have it; al-Zawzani's text lacks it.

translation: Women in litters of Jusham ibn Bakr,
who have joined to beauty both lineage and faith.
97.sharh: The women are of the poet's own clan, Jusham ibn Bakr, and combine good looks with noble birth and piety, as al-Zawzani explains: the same union of beauty and virtue he praised in his beloved.

translation: Nothing guards the women like the kind of blows
that send forearms flying like tip-cat sticks.
98.sharh: The best protection for the women is fierce swordplay that sends severed forearms flying like the sticks in a boys' game of tip-cat. Only the sword, not words or pledges, keeps them safe.

translation: When swords are drawn, it is as if
we had fathered all mankind together.
99.sharh: In time of war Taghlib protects everyone as a father protects his children, as al-Zawzani explains the image. The line is in al-Zawzani and the Jamhara but not in Ibn al-Anbari.

translation: They roll heads along as burly lads
roll their balls on the level ground.
100.sharh: Taghlib's warriors send enemy heads rolling as easily as strong boys knock balls about on a flat, pebbly valley floor, as al-Zawzani explains. The line is in al-Zawzani and the Jamhara only.

translation: The tribes of Ma'add well know,
when tents are pitched in the valley floor,
101.sharh: This opens a long run of lines, each beginning “that we...”, listing what all the tribes know of Taghlib. Abu Ja'far, quoted by Ibn al-Anbari, takes the valley to be that of Mecca, where people gathered from every side.

translation: that we are the protectors in every year of drought,
and the givers to all who come asking,
102.sharh: First on the list: in famine years Taghlib shelters the weak and gives freely to anyone who comes for help. Generosity heads the list, before strength in war.

translation: that we feed others when we have the means,
and destroy when we are put to the test,
103.sharh: Taghlib feeds guests whenever it can and destroys any enemy who tries its strength. Al-Tibrizi and the Jamhara read “we are generous when we have the upper hand, and destroy when we are attacked”.

translation: that we withhold whatever we choose,
and camp wherever we please,
104.sharh: No one can take from Taghlib what it chooses to keep, or keep it from any land it wants to camp on, as al-Zawzani explains. The Jamhara reads “we rule as we will”.

translation: that we defend those who live near us
when swords have left their scabbards,
105.sharh: When the swords come out, Taghlib protects its neighbours, at the moment others abandon theirs. Ibn al-Anbari has “parted from” where the reciter says “left”; the meaning is the same.

translation: that we refuse when we are displeased,
and accept when we are content,
106.sharh: Al-Zawzani explains: Taghlib will take no gift from anyone it is angry with, and accepts the presents of those it favours. Line 76 says much the same in other words: the recited text keeps overlapping lines from two recensions.

translation: that we protect when we are obeyed,
and are fierce when we are defied,
107.sharh: Those who obey Taghlib are safe under its protection; those who defy it meet its full ferocity. The reciter's word, “fierce”, is the text of a printed edition of the Jamhara; al-Zawzani has “resolute”.

translation: that we pursue when we are wronged,
and strike when we are put to the test,
108.sharh: Whoever offends Taghlib is hunted down, and any challenge is met with the sword, as al-Durra explains. The line is one of the Jamhara's, not in the classical commentaries.

translation: that we camp at every frontier
where those who camp fear death,
109.sharh: Taghlib settles even on the most dangerous borderlands, exposed to enemy raids, where other tribes fear for their lives, as al-Durra explains. The line is in the Jamhara.

translation: and we drink clear water when we come to it,
while others drink it muddied and thick.
110.sharh: Taghlib is always first at the well, so it drinks the water clean while others get the dregs. Ibn al-Anbari says the water stands for everything: they take the best of all things.

translation: Carry word from us to the Banu al-Tammah
and to Du'mi: how did you find us?
111.sharh: He taunts two clans Taghlib has fought, the Banu al-Tammah and Du'mi: let them say how Taghlib dealt with them, as brave men or cowards. Ibn al-Anbari makes both clans of Iyad.

translation: When a king imposes humiliation on people,
we refuse to let disgrace settle among us.
112.sharh: Other tribes may bow when a king forces shame on them; Taghlib refuses. Al-Zawzani: when a king compels people to what humbles them, we will not be led.

translation: The world is ours and all who live on it,
and when we strike, we strike with power.
113.sharh: The boast reaches its widest: the whole world and its people belong to Taghlib, and it strikes whenever it chooses, with nothing to hold it back. Ibn al-Anbari says only some transmitters had this line.

translation: Aggressors, wrongdoers, though no one wronged us,
but we will be the first to do wrong.
114.sharh: A defiant boast: no one has dared wrong Taghlib, so it will strike first. Al-Tibrizi's reading turns it: “we are called wrongdoers though we have wronged no one, but we will start”.

translation: The two Mus'abs and the clan of Bakr called to one another,
and they cried, “To us, Kinda, all of you!”
115.sharh: The enemy rallied: two allied clans, the Mus'abs, together with Bakr, called out for help from the whole tribe of Kinda. This line and the next come from the Jamhara; the classical commentators do not have them.

translation: If we win, we have always been winners,
and if we lose, we are not ones who are often beaten.
116.sharh: Victory is Taghlib's habit; a defeat would be a mere turn of fortune, not a sign of weakness. Ibn Hisham's Sira and al-Baghdadi's Khizana give the line to Farwa ibn Musayk of Murad, in verses on a battle between Murad and Hamdan; the Jamhara puts it in this poem.

translation: We filled the land till it was too narrow for us,
and the sea we fill with ships.
117.sharh: Taghlib's numbers cover the land until it cannot hold them, and its ships cover the sea. Ibn al-Anbari allows “the sea” to be read as object or subject of the clause.

translation: When a boy of ours reaches weaning,
tyrants fall down before him on their faces.
118.sharh: Even a Taghlib infant, barely weaned, makes mighty men prostrate themselves, as al-Zawzani puts it: the tyrants of other peoples bow to their children. The recording ends here.

1.1.2.meaning: Get up, wake: from habba, to start up out of sleep.

1.1.3.head: صَحن
1.1.3.meaning: Sahn: a large, wide drinking bowl.

1.1.4.head: اِصبَحي
1.1.4.meaning: Pour us the sabuh, the morning draught of wine.

1.2.4.head: الأَندَرين
1.2.4.meaning: Al-Andarin: a village in Syria known for its wine; Harun, the editor of Ibn al-Anbari, places it south of Aleppo.

2.1.1.head: مُشَعشَع
2.1.1.meaning: Mixed with water and so made thin and clear.

2.1.3.head: الحُصّ
2.1.3.meaning: Huss: the plant called wars, whose red flowers look like saffron; it was used as a dye.

3.1.3.meaning: Lubana: a need, a pressing wish.

5.1.2.head: الشِّهاب
5.1.2.meaning: Shuhub: flames, burning brands; also shooting stars.

6.1.4-5.meaning: Umm Amr, “mother of Amr”: the woman pouring the wine; the Jamhara's commentary says she is the poet's own mother.

8.2.4.head: قاصِرين
8.2.4.meaning: Qasirin: a town that stood near Balis, according to Yaqut.

9.1.3.head: حُمَيّا
9.1.3.meaning: Humayya: the heat and sting of wine as it rises to the head.

12.1.5.head: ظَعينَة
12.1.5.meaning: Za'ina: a woman travelling in a camel litter; the vocative drops its final ending.

14.2.1.meaning: “Cooled (the eyes)”: made glad, gave them what they longed for.

14.2.3.head: مَولى
14.2.3.meaning: Your mawali: here, your cousins and kinsmen.

15.1.5.meaning: Rahn: a pledge, something held and bound.

16.2.4.head: الكاشِح
16.2.4.meaning: Kashih: a secret enemy, one who turns his flank on you.

17.1.2.meaning: Aytal: a she-camel with a long neck.

17.2.3-5.meaning: “Has never gathered a foetus”: has never been pregnant.

18.1.3.head: حُقّ
18.1.3.meaning: Huqq: a small round box with a lid.

19.2.3.head: مُدجِن
19.2.3.meaning: In the dark (dujna). The Jamhara has mudlijina, “travelling by night”.

21.1.1.head: مَأكَمَة
21.1.1.meaning: Ma'kama: the top of the hip.

23.1.5.meaning: Saqb: a newborn male camel calf.

24.1.2.meaning: Shamta': a woman whose hair has turned grey.

24.2.5.head: جَنين
24.2.5.meaning: Janin: “hidden”; here, buried in the grave.

25.2.2.head: حُمول
25.2.2.meaning: Humul: laden camels carrying the litters and baggage.

25.2.4.head: حَدا
25.2.4.meaning: Driven on with the camel-drivers' song.

26.1.2.meaning: Al-Yamama: a region counted as part of Najd, with Hajr as its chief town, according to Yaqut.

27.1.1-2.meaning: Abu Hind: the kunya of Amr ibn Hind, king of al-Hira.

28.1.2.head: أَورَدَ
28.1.2.meaning: We lead down to water: here, into battle.

29.1.3.head: أَغَرّ
29.1.3.meaning: Ghurr: “white-blazed”, like horses with a blaze; famous.

30.2.4.head: المُحجَر
30.2.4.meaning: Those driven into a corner, who seek refuge.

31.2.1-2.meaning: “With their reins for necklaces”: reins looped over their necks, the riders having dismounted.

31.2.3.head: صافِن
31.2.3.meaning: Standing on three legs, the fourth hoof tipped up: the stance of a resting horse.

32.1.4.head: ذو طُلوح
32.1.4.meaning: Dhu Tuluh: a place in the uplands of Banu Yarbu' between Kufa and Fayd, according to Yaqut.

32.2.3.head: نَفى
32.2.3.meaning: Drives off. Al-Zawzani and the Jamhara have nanfi, “we drive off”.

33.2.2.meaning: Qatada: a thorny desert shrub, tragacanth.

34.1.5.head: رَحى
34.1.5.meaning: Raha: a millstone; here, the full force of war.

35.1.2.head: ثِفال
35.1.2.meaning: Thifal: the hide or cloth spread under a hand-mill to catch the flour.

35.2.1.head: لُهوَة
35.2.1.meaning: Luhwa: the handful of grain dropped into a mill.

36.2.2.meaning: Qira: the meal given to a guest.

37.2.3.meaning: Mirdat: a heavy stone for breaking rocks.

40.1.4.head: الخَطِّيّ
40.1.4.meaning: Khatti: spears named after al-Khatt, a place on the coast of Bahrain, according to al-Bakri.

40.2.4.head: اِختَلى
40.2.4.meaning: They mow, as fresh grass is cut.

44.1.5.head: مَعَدّ
44.1.5.meaning: Ma'add: the northern Arab tribes descended from Ma'add ibn Adnan.

45.2.2.head: الحَفض
45.2.2.meaning: Ahfad: baggage camels, or the household goods they carry.

47.2.1.head: مِخراق
47.2.1.meaning: Mikhraq: a cloth twisted into a club for boys' games.

49.1.4.head: الإِسناف
49.1.4.meaning: Isnaf: pressing forward, advancing into battle.

50.1.3.meaning: Rahwa: a mountain, or high ground.

52.1.1.meaning: Hudayya: a challenge; the word has the shape of a diminutive.

54.2.3.head: مُتَلَبِّب
54.2.3.meaning: Girded for battle, in full armour.

55.1.4-6.meaning: Jusham ibn Bakr: the poet's own clan of Taghlib.

55.2.3-4.meaning: The plains and the rough ground: here, the weak and the strong.

57.1.3.head: جَهِلَ
57.1.3.meaning: Act rashly, insolently: jahl here is hot-headed folly, not ignorance.

58.1.3-5.meaning: Amr ibn Hind: Amr son of al-Mundhir, king of al-Hira, known by his mother's name.

58.2.2.head: قَيل
58.2.2.meaning: Qayl: a lesser king, a ruler under an overlord.

61.2.4.head: مَقتَوِيّ
61.2.4.meaning: Maqtawin: servants, especially those who serve kings.

62.1.2.head: قَناة
62.1.2.meaning: Qanat: a spear shaft; a figure for strength and pride.

63.1.3.meaning: Thiqaf: the iron clamp used to straighten spear shafts.

63.2.3.head: زَبون
63.2.3.meaning: Zabun: kicking, thrusting away, like a camel that kicks the milker.

66.1.3-5.meaning: Alqama ibn Sayf: a man of Taghlib, said to have led the tribe into al-Jazira, according to al-Tibrizi.

67.1.2.head: مُهَلهِل
67.1.2.meaning: Muhalhil: Muhalhil ibn Rabi'a, brother of Kulayb and father of the poet's mother Layla.

67.2.1.head: زُهَير
67.2.1.meaning: Zuhayr: a man of Taghlib, as Ibn al-Anbari says; al-Tibrizi calls him the poet's forefather on his father's side, and the lineage in al-Aghani runs through Zuhayr ibn Jusham.

68.1.2.head: كُلثوم
68.1.2.meaning: Kulthum: Kulthum ibn Malik, the poet's father.

69.1.1-2.head: ذو البُرَة
69.1.1-2.meaning: Dhu al-Bura, “the man with the ring”: a chief of Taghlib, nicknamed, Abu Ja'far says in Ibn al-Anbari, for a curl of hair on his nose, round like a ring (bura).

70.1.4.meaning: Kulayb: Kulayb ibn Rabi'a, called Kulayb of Wa'il, brother of Muhalhil; his murder set off a long war between Taghlib and Bakr.

72.1.4.head: ذِمار
72.1.4.meaning: Dhimar: whatever a man is bound in honour to protect.

73.1.5.meaning: Khazaza: a mountain, scene of the battle of Khazaz between the northern tribes of Nizar and the Yemenis; Abu Ziyad, quoted by Yaqut, calls it the greatest battle of pre-Islamic Arabia.

74.1.4.head: ذو أُراطى
74.1.4.meaning: Dhu Urata: a place, or a watering place; Yaqut lists the day of Urata among the battles of the Arabs.

77.2.3-4.meaning: “The sons of our father”: their brother tribe Bakr; Taghlib and Bakr were both sons of Wa'il.

80.1.4.meaning: Bakr: Bakr ibn Wa'il, Taghlib's brother tribe and rival before the king.

83.1.3.head: اليَلَب
83.1.3.meaning: Yalab: armour of woven leather thongs.

84.1.3.meaning: Sabigha: a long, full coat of mail.

85.2.5.head: جَون
85.2.5.meaning: Jun: black; the word can also mean white, but black is meant here.

86.1.4.head: غَدير
86.1.4.meaning: Ghudr: pools left by a flood.

87.1.4.head: أَجرَد
87.1.4.meaning: Jurd: short-haired horses, a mark of good breeding.

87.2.3.head: نَقيذَة
87.2.3.meaning: Naqa'idh: horses rescued from the enemy.

88.2.2.head: الرَّصيعَة
88.2.2.meaning: Rasa'i': the knots of a horse's reins.

91.2.4.head: مُعلِم
91.2.4.meaning: Wearing a mark of distinction in battle, as champions did.

92.1.1.head: اِستَلَبَ
92.1.1.meaning: You will surely carry off: the women speak to their men. The commentaries and the Jamhara have la-yastalibunna, “they will surely carry off”.

92.1.3.head: أَبيَض
92.1.3.meaning: White ones: swords, as al-Zawzani vowels it. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Tibrizi have abdanan, “coats of mail”, for “horses”; read baydan, the word means helmets.

95.1.1.head: قاتَ
95.1.1.meaning: They feed: from qut, daily fodder or food.

98.2.4.head: القُلَة
98.2.4.meaning: Qulin: the short sticks of a boys' game, struck into the air with a longer stick.

102.1.4.meaning: Kahl: a year of drought and hunger.

111.1.4.head: بَنو الطَّمّاح
111.1.4.meaning: Banu al-Tammah: a clan of Iyad according to Ibn al-Anbari, of Wa'il according to Ibn al-Sikkit.

111.2.1.head: دُعمِيّ
111.2.1.meaning: Du'mi: Du'mi ibn Jadila, a clan of Iyad.

113.1.4.meaning: Is (literally “is at evening”), lives. Ibn al-Anbari's text has wa-ma amsa, “and whatever is”, but his editor's manuscript M has wa-man amsa, as recited, and so does al-Hashimi's Jawahir al-Adab; al-Tibrizi and the Jamhara have wa-man adha.

115.1.2.meaning: Al-Mus'aban, “the two Mus'abs”: not identified by the commentators; Ibn al-Kalbi records two clans of that name, of Murad or of al-Azd, but whether they are meant here is unknown.

115.2.2-3.meaning: “O for Kinda”: a cry for help to Kinda, the tribe of the poet Imru' al-Qays.
